Earn points and command woodland creatures by having the most birds on a location, pushing your foes off the perch, and breaking ties to take the lead. Each round, players add their birds into a shared bag. Players then draw birds of their own, and other players take turns stacking birds on location tiles. Each location tile will award variable points for majorities and sometimes grant players a unique ability. The game ends after five rounds, and the player who has earned the most points wins. With a modular tile configuration and a variety of woodland creatures to control, each game will present a new tactical challenge. Discover Board Game Arena Rules summary Contents 1 Setup 2 Migration Phase 3 Recruit Phase 4 Perch Phase 5 Upkeep Phase 6 End Game Scoring Setup Each player receives 2 objective cards and must keep one. Migration Phase Each player places 2 of their birds in the migration bag. Recruit Phase Each player receives 2 of their birds and also draw 2 random birds from the migration bag. Perch Phase This is the main phase of the game. Each player takes turn placing exactly one bird on one of the tiles. Birds must be stacked on top of other birds of the same color. Placing a bird in a nest counts as one more bird of that color on the tile. Before or after placing a bird, the player may use a bonus action: Place a birdhouse. This counts as one more bird and protects the birds from effects of creatures, zap and placing more birds of that color. Zap a bird. Remove a bird from any tile and send them to the fountain. Activate a creature. Each creature can only be activated once per Perch Phase. When all players have placed all their birds, the Perch Phase ends. Upkeep Phase Each location is scored: the player with the most birds scores the first points on the tile, the second most scores the second points, and the third most scores the third points. Ties cancels each other. The turn order is then determined: this player with the highest score goes first, the second highest goes second, and so on. In case of a tie, the player with that arrived first at that score is considered first. Creature are made available. Trigger tiles with upkeep effects. Advance the round marker. At the start of the 4th round, players gain a birdhouse. On the 5th round, players gain a zap token. At the end of the 5th round, the game ends. If the game has not ended, a new Migration Phase starts. End Game Scoring Birds in the migration bag are send to the plaza. Each player reveals their objective card and scores points accordingly. The player with the largest flock on a single tile scores 10 points. Each controlled tile scores 3 points to their controller. Each bird on the fountain scores points according to their height. Each bird on the plaza scores 1 point. The player with the most points wins. In case of a tie, the player with the most birdson a single tile wins. In case of a tie, the player with the most birds on the fountain wins. If still tied, the players share the victory. [Rating: 3/10] Playing 5 rounds makes this last way too long and it quickly becomes dull. Area majority isn't my favourite mechanism and this game shows why: the movements are often zero sum tit for tat; and because there's no clearing between rounds, the lead on each location is often static. There's hardly any bag building: getting to place your opponents' pieces can be useful but it's entirely tactical because the draw is largely random. The animal powers supposedly mix this up, yet they all feel similar, their impact is marginal, and can be reversed if you're not last in turn order.

[Rating: 4/10] I guess it's a good gateway game and MARVELLOUS ILLUSTRATIONS but  1. Bit too random with the objectives  2. Too fiddly, both with rule/setup changes, just like a Euro and with the components   3. What's the point of having special animal powers if control isn't dynamic & it is only once per round?   4. Didn't feel like there was any good way to catch up & there were no twists in who was leading— this is usually almost the case in area control games, but wasn't so here.   5. The designer seems to have wanted to just include a cool mean rule of "no one scores if tied". In the 3P game we played,

Maybe I was playing with folks that took too long to play but I did not like it.
